claims.claimText: King's College London does not require students to cite generative AI as an authoritative source in the reference list, but it requires students to acknowledge any use of generative AI tools in coursework by including a declaration statement with their references. Unless the assessment brief gives other wording, students append either a declaration that no part of the submission was generated by AI software (English grammar and spell checking is consistent with this statement) or a declaration that parts of the submission have AI contributions within the acceptable use specified in the brief, naming the tools and how they were used.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: King’s College London, unlike some other universities, does not require students to reference generative AI as an authoritative source in the reference list for much the same reason you would not be expected to cite a search engine, a student essay website or be over-dependent on synoptic, secondary source material.

claims.claimText: King's Academic Misconduct Policy states that using generative AI tools to produce output that is then copied as part of a submission is not appropriate, that any work submitted must genuinely demonstrate the student's own work, skills and knowledge and follow the assessment guidelines, and that generative AI writing programmes are third-party technologies to be used only in accordance with College guidance. The King's guidance adds that submitting AI-generated text as one's own without written departmental permission is considered misconduct (third-party involvement or text manipulation) where it gives undue advantage or interferes with assessment of the student's own understanding. A written permission or acknowledgement does not by itself make substantive AI content creation acceptable.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: However, the use of generative AI tools to produce output which is then copied as part of a submission is not appropriate. Prudent, ethical and constructive use of tools is increasingly likely to form part of the production of assessed work.
evidence.snippetLocation: Academic Misconduct Policy s4.2; physical PDF page 4; lines 172-174 of captured PDF text

claims.claimText: King's College London suggests four broad levels of generative AI use in assessment that programme and module leaders may adjust to each assessment: Minimal (routine tools such as auto transcription, spell and grammar checkers), Limited/selective (clearly delineated tasks as allowed), Open (no specific restrictions but key stages and tools must be tracked) and Embedded (AI use is a focal part of the assessment). The levels are a framework for the actual assessment brief, not an automatic university-wide permission, and verbatim use of generated content without acknowledgement is never appropriate.

claims.claimText: King's Academic Misconduct Policy distinguishes poor academic practice from academic misconduct: an ASB Chair may decide a concern is an unintentional misunderstanding of scholarly practice (for example incomplete citation), which is not misconduct; the student receives feedback and the work is marked against the criteria. Blatant, extensive or careless failures are excluded from this category.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Once the ASB Chair (or their nominee) has reviewed the information available, they may decide that the concern relates to poor academic practice and that no academic misconduct has occurred. Poor academic practice involves an unintentional misunderstanding of scholarly practice. Examples include when sources are acknowledged to some extent, but citation is inadequate or incomplete. It does not include when the failure to adhere to scholarly practice is blatant, extensive or results from a lack of effort. Poor academic practice is not a form of academic misconduct.
evidence.snippetLocation: Academic Misconduct Policy s7.4; physical PDF page 8; lines 365-372 of captured PDF text

claims.claimText: Under King's Academic Misconduct Policy, a suspected case normally goes first to a Stage One Academic Integrity Meeting (AIM) with two staff members. The AIM is not a hearing and should be informal, supportive and exploratory; where authorship or third-party involvement is in doubt the student may be asked to explain their answers, ideas or references, but must not be pressured or obliged to give specific responses and may respond in writing instead. Staff share their notes, and the student may add information, normally within 5 working days. Possible Stage One outcomes are no concern, poor academic practice, a local educative or restorative outcome, or referral to a Stage Two Misconduct Committee.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The student will be invited to attend the Academic Integrity Meeting (AIM), which will normally be with any two of the following staff members: module leader, programme leader (or deputy), ASB Chair (or nominee), Programme Manager or personal tutor.

claims.claimText: King's Academic Misconduct Policy provides two different review routes with different start points. Where a Stage One AIM finds misconduct and applies a local penalty (Outcome 3), the student may send a contestation in writing to Student Conduct & Appeals within 10 working days from the date of written notification of the Stage One outcome. A Stage Two Misconduct Committee decision may be appealed, on the grounds of new evidence or significant procedural error, by submitting a Misconduct Appeal Form within 10 working days of the date of the Misconduct Committee outcome. Possible outcomes range from educative measures such as a formal warning or capped resubmission to punitive outcomes up to suspension or expulsion; AI use does not carry an automatic penalty.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: In the case of Outcome 3 (see 7.13), where academic misconduct has been found and a penalty applied by the ASB Chair, the student may contest this outcome.

claims.claimText: King's guidance for AI-assisted marking and feedback (July 2025) says staff should never upload student work to any AI system without explicit consent and forethought, should not include student details or upload work into any GenAI tool without explicit permission, should use approved or supported university GenAI tools, and should keep reading and assessing student work primarily human with human oversight. Staff should not use GenAI tools to detect students' use of GenAI. This guidance governs staff marking and data handling; it is not a rule about students' own AI use.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Importantly, it does make clear that we should never upload student work to any AI system without explicit consent and forethought.
